Slight deduction for being a somewhat familiar 'sexism gets its comeuppance' structure, but the execution is crisp.

jokes.text: Ted Nightingale's retort to Veronica's ratings burn: 'Ouch. Don't lose any more hair over it.'
jokes.setup: Veronica has just landed a solid ratings comeback.
jokes.punchline: The rival fires back with an insult about hair loss — implying he's going bald and trying to deflect — a petty, weak riposte that reveals he has no good answer.
jokes.explanation: Generic physical-appearance insult with minimal wit. The joke is that his comeback is weak (which is intentional — he's losing the exchange), but it doesn't elevate beyond a low-craft retort. Functions as a coda to joke #9 but adds little on its own.

jokes.text: Ted Nightingale begins reporting on the panda birth, starts singing 'Afternoon Delight,' then mid-lyric substitutes: '♪ I make fart noises with my mouth ♪'
jokes.setup: A rival anchor is delivering a seemingly professional live report at the zoo.
jokes.punchline: He inexplicably breaks into song, and replaces the actual lyric with an infantile non-sequitur about making fart noises, undermining any professional credibility entirely.
jokes.explanation: The substituted lyric is a great absurdist pivot — from romantic song to the most childish possible boast. The commitment to the melody while singing something idiotic is a classic McKay improvisational move. Works well, especially the abrupt interruption that follows.

jokes.text: Ron, in a bar, shouts back at the bartender who told him to quit singing: 'I'm expressing my inner anguish through the majesty of song!'
jokes.setup: Ron has been singing loudly and badly in a bar, bothering patrons. The bartender tells him to stop.
jokes.punchline: Ron's defense — 'the majesty of song' — frames his drunken caterwauling in grandiose artistic terms. The gap between the description and the reality is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Burgundy register: everything he does is elevated in his mind to 'majesty.' This is character comedy at a high level — only Ron would describe his drunken bar singing with this kind of self-regard. 'The majesty of song' is quotable and perfectly in his voice.

jokes.text: Bar patron: 'Hey, nut job! Quit the singin'! Creeping out all the regulars.'
jokes.setup: Ron is singing loudly and badly in a bar in full breakdown mode
jokes.punchline: The patron's concern is not Ron's mental state, not his suffering — it's that he's 'creeping out the regulars,' a purely practical complaint about bar atmosphere
jokes.explanation: Functional supporting joke — the contrast between Ron's epic suffering and the mundane complaint about regular customers is the core of the joke. Competent but not distinguished.

jokes.text: Ron's breakdown confession to the bartender: 'She's better than me!' — followed by a long pause and then quieter: 'She's better than me.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been ranting about Veronica, calling her a 'she-devil.' The bartender suggests he'll have to deal with women being capable.
jokes.punchline: Ron's dawning, anguished admission — 'she's better than me' — said twice, the second time with broken resignation, is both the emotional nadir and the comedic peak of Ron's arc. His ego's complete collapse is played for genuine laughs.
jokes.explanation: This is earned comedy. The entire first act of the film has been about Ron's towering self-regard, so watching it crumble in a bar over the word 'better' — said twice, with the second repetition being quieter and more devastated — is both funny and weirdly poignant. The repetition is the structure: first time is shock, second time is confirmation. Strong character integration: this is the precise wound for Ron Burgundy.

jokes.text: Bartender's sage advice: 'You know, times are changing. Ladies can do stuff now. You're gonna have to learn how to deal with that.' Ron: 'What? Were you saying something? Look, I don't speak Spanish.'
jokes.setup: The bartender offers genuinely reasonable advice about gender equality.
jokes.punchline: Ron literally does not absorb a word of it, claiming he 'doesn't speak Spanish' — the bartender was speaking plain English. Ron's willful, oblivious deflection is funnier than any actual rebuttal could be.
jokes.explanation: Ron's 'I don't speak Spanish' is a great absurdist non-sequitur but it's also deeply character-specific: he genuinely cannot process information that challenges his worldview, so his brain rejects it as a foreign language. This is thematically resonant and funny simultaneously. The bartender's reasonable advice hitting an impenetrable wall of narcissism is the core comedic engine of Ron's character.

jokes.text: A public television reporter flirts with Veronica at the zoo under the pretense of professional solidarity: 'We at public television, we're really down with the woman's lib thing.' Veronica finds it 'refreshing.'
jokes.setup: A male reporter approaches Veronica, ostensibly to share camera positioning.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to performative feminist ally-ship as a flirtation tactic, and Veronica begins to fall for the flattery — the irony being that every man trying to 'help' Veronica has an ulterior motive.
jokes.explanation: Competent satirical joke about performative male feminism, but the payoff is interrupted before it completes (Howie steals the shot). Works more as setup for the next beat than as a standalone joke. Moderate craft.

jokes.text: While the public TV reporter is mid-schmooze, Howie (from another crew) leans past Veronica, steals the camera shot position, whispers 'Don't want to wake up your friends' — implying Veronica and the reporter are literally asleep or gullible.
jokes.setup: Public TV reporter thinks he's smooth-talked his way into Veronica's good graces and secured the shot.
jokes.punchline: A third party simply swoops in and takes the position, implying that Veronica's professional rivals are playing her while she's distracted by flattery.
jokes.explanation: Decent visual/situational comedy — the rug-pull of Howie exploiting the moment is well-constructed. 'Don't want to wake up your friends' is a smug kicker that works. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Ed Harken, in total crisis mode: 'I can't believe I'm about to do this' — then calls Ron Burgundy's bar.
jokes.setup: Harken is desperate — Corningstone has vanished and the panda birth is live. He needs an anchor.
jokes.punchline: His agonized admission that calling Ron is worse than the alternative — including 'I'd rather slit my throat' — reveals just how low Ron's stock has fallen, and how bad this situation is.
jokes.explanation: 'I'd rather slit my throat' is a darkly comic aside that works because Harken is so deadpan about it. Good character work — Harken's antipathy toward Ron is well-established, so this lands. Not exceptional but solid.

jokes.text: Phone call between Harken and Ron at the bar: 'Is there an anchorman there?' / 'Hold on.' Then Ron can't figure out who 'Ed' is — 'Who is this?' / 'Ed Harken!' / 'I don't know a Ned.'
jokes.setup: Harken, humiliated, calls a bar to retrieve Ron Burgundy.
jokes.punchline: Ron — drunk, broken — can't even recognize the name of his long-time boss. 'I don't know a Ned' is the peak of Ron's oblivious incompetence meeting alcohol.
jokes.explanation: Classic drunk-confusion comedy with good character specificity. The 'Is there an anchorman there?' ask is itself funny — implying it's a legitimate question for this bar. 'I don't know a Ned' is a nicely dumb mishearing that extends the beat perfectly without over-staying.

jokes.text: Ron's reaction to being asked back: 'Ed! That's wonderful! Thank you! Ed, hold on. I want to say a few words. You have always been a good friend! Always!' while Ed just keeps saying 'Right. Right.'
jokes.setup: Harken, clearly not Ron's friend and doing this under duress, asks Ron to come back.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately begins an emotional speech about their 'friendship' while Harken flatly responds 'Right. Right.' — the gap between Ron's sentimentality and Harken's boredom is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Ron's emotional lavishing of affection on someone who clearly cannot stand him, with Harken's dismissive 'Right. Right.' as counterpoint, is a good two-hander. Harken's restraint is the punchline. The 'Always!' with its emotional peak is particularly good — Ron inhabiting a friendship entirely in his own head.

jokes.text: Ron's final words to Harken before hanging up: 'Ed, I'll be down there. And I'm going to look good.'
jokes.setup: Harken has urgently asked Ron to get to the zoo immediately for the biggest story of the year.
jokes.punchline: Ron's priority — out of everything he could say — is to reassure Ed that he will look good. His vanity is so ingrained it surfaces even in a moment of professional redemption.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character economy. Five words. 'I'm going to look good' — in a crisis — is entirely Ron. The simplicity is the craft: it doesn't need explaining, it doesn't need a reaction shot, it just IS Ron Burgundy condensed to a single sentence. Excellent economy score.

jokes.text: Ron appears at the bar door (or on the street) freshly groomed in his anchor suit; a bystander says: 'Damn! That dude cleans up good!'
jokes.setup: Ron has just been a disheveled, drunk mess.
jokes.punchline: He appears immaculately groomed — the speed of his transformation is itself the joke. The bystander's street-vernacular appreciation ('That dude cleans up good!') adds to the comedy by treating Ron's re-anchorization as a neighborhood spectacle.
jokes.explanation: Good visual beat. The instantaneous transition from wreck to anchor god is a reliable comedy principle (absurd speed of change). The bystander's reaction is a nice touch of community investment in Ron's appearance. Solid if not exceptional.

jokes.text: Ron, standing alone and striking a pose: 'News team! Assemble!' — then walks to an entirely empty street. He shouts again: 'News team, assemble!'
jokes.setup: Ron issues his rallying cry to the news team, expecting them to materialize around him.
jokes.punchline: No one comes. He yells it again, apparently unperturbed, the absurdity of a man shouting 'assemble' into an empty street played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The 'Avengers assemble' parody of authority works because Ron's self-regard is so total that he genuinely expects this to work like a superhero summons. The gap between expectation and empty street is well-timed. The double-shout without acknowledgment or embarrassment is the right choice.

jokes.text: News team appears behind Ron; when he discovers them: 'Oh. Hi. Didn't see you there.' Brian: 'We've been here literally the entire time you have.' Ron: 'I'm a little embarrassed.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been dramatically calling out into empty space; the team has apparently been right there.
jokes.punchline: His entire dramatic summoning was performed in front of people who were watching him the whole time. 'I'm a little embarrassed' is so understated as to be perfect — Ron being slightly embarrassed rather than mortified.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the previous beat. 'We've been here literally the entire time you have' is a great straight-man line, and 'I'm a little embarrassed' is exactly the right degree of underreaction. Ron's self-awareness is calibrated precisely: a small amount, just enough to register, not enough to change anything. Well-structured two-beat comedy.

jokes.text: Brian's melodramatic response to Ron's ask: 'That was half a lifetime ago. We're different people now. When you left, the hurt was so deep. I don't know if I can go through that again. Think about what you're asking.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks his news team to come back with him for one more story.
jokes.punchline: Brian responds as though Ron has asked him to return to a traumatic long-term relationship, complete with 'the hurt was so deep' — treating a brief professional exile as a devastating romantic abandonment.
jokes.explanation: Good comic escalation of the news team's emotional investment in Ron. Brian's soap-opera register — 'the hurt was so deep' — for a workplace separation is funny and consistent with the film's thesis that these men treat local news as their entire cosmic identity. 'Think about what you're asking' is a solid punchline beat.

jokes.text: Champ's response to Ron's 'will you follow me again?': 'I'm gettin' too old for this shit.' Then: 'To the news van!'
jokes.setup: Ron delivers his stirring rallying speech. The team is moved.
jokes.punchline: Champ quotes 'I'm getting too old for this shit' — the Lethal Weapon cliché — before immediately and enthusiastically yelling 'To the news van!' The irony is he's the most excited person there despite the protest.
jokes.explanation: The Lethal Weapon quote is a bit of an easy cultural reference, but its deployment here is correct — it's self-aware about being a cliché while Champ himself doesn't realize it. The pivot to immediate enthusiasm ('To the news van!') is the stronger element. Functional but leans on borrowed material.

jokes.text: News team arrives at the zoo in their van; strangers recognize Ron and cheer: 'Well, I'll be. Ron Burgundy. He's back!'
jokes.setup: The news team pulls up to the zoo for the big story.
jokes.punchline: Random San Diegans treat Ron Burgundy's arrival like a local hero's return — the joke being that a local news anchor inspires this level of devotion.
jokes.explanation: Pleasant running joke about Ron's local celebrity status. The fan recognition is a consistent comedic element of the film. Functions as world-building comedy — reinforcing how outsized Ron's local fame is. Not particularly inventive but lands reliably.

jokes.text: Ron hears Veronica's voice calling for help from the bear pit — 'Ron, help!' — then immediately says 'Wait! Did you just hear something?'
jokes.setup: Veronica is apparently trapped in the bear enclosure calling for help.
jokes.punchline: Ron's reaction to a voice clearly saying 'Ron, help!' is to ask 'Wait! Did you just hear something?' — as if the cry for help was ambiguous. His processing speed for crises affecting others is glacial.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Ron's obliviousness to obvious signals is a reliable comedic engine. 'Did you just hear something?' when someone has literally said his name is the right degree of density. Sets up the more elaborate dilemma joke that follows.

jokes.text: Team member's attempt to diplomatically frame the dilemma: 'Whoa, Ron, I don't want to sound cruel, but — there's a network talent scout over there.' Ron: 'This is a tough decision.'
jokes.setup: Veronica is in immediate danger in a bear pit.
jokes.punchline: The news team member — trying not to 'sound cruel' — immediately points out the talent scout, and Ron declares it 'a tough decision.' Saving a human life vs. a career opportunity should not be a 'tough decision.'
jokes.explanation: 'I don't want to sound cruel, but' is a perfect setup because it acknowledges the cruelty while proceeding with it anyway. The collective moral corruption of this news team — prioritizing career over life — is played entirely straight and is very funny. Good character integration for the 'us vs. the story' mentality of TV journalists.

jokes.text: Ron's internal monologue aloud: 'Basically the biggest story of my career, launching me to a level I've never known before — or saving the woman I used to have familiar relations with. This is hard! I am in a pickle!'
jokes.setup: Ron is weighing his options with Veronica trapped in the bear pit.
jokes.punchline: 'The woman I used to have familiar relations with' — Ron's euphemism for the woman he loves, which he uses even in an urgent crisis. The exclamation 'I am in a pickle!' treats a life-or-death emergency with the gravity of a minor inconvenience.
jokes.explanation: Ron's vocabulary choices are the joke: 'familiar relations' and 'I am in a pickle' are anchored in an earlier era of genteel euphemism, which contrasts with the urgency. 'I am in a pickle' for 'my girlfriend is being eaten by bears' is perfect character-specific comedy. The phrasing could only be Ron Burgundy.

jokes.text: Team member's sincere theological reasoning: 'Ron, I know it sounds harsh, but God does not want her to live.'
jokes.setup: The team is advising Ron on whether to save Veronica.
jokes.punchline: The confident invocation of divine will — 'God does not want her to live' — to justify abandoning someone in a bear pit is a casually monstrous non-sequitur delivered as reasonable counsel.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. Its power is in its brevity and total commitment: no hedging, no irony in the delivery, just 'God does not want her to live' as a reasonable position. The 'I know it sounds harsh' acknowledgment followed by complete theological certainty is structurally brilliant. High originality — it's a unique line, not a variation on anything familiar. Genuinely quotable and darkly funny.

jokes.text: Ron jumps into the bear pit, immediately says: 'I immediately regret this decision.'
jokes.setup: Ron heroically leaps into the bear pit to save Veronica.
jokes.punchline: The instant he lands, still in the same breath as the heroic act, he announces his regret. The speed of the reversal — zero pause between action and second-guessing — is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and a perfect five-word joke. Its craft is in the structure: the heroic gesture and the regret are simultaneous, so the courage and the cowardice exist at the same instant. 'I immediately regret this decision' has the clinical formality of Ron's anchor-speak ('I immediately' instead of 'I already') applied to raw panic. Near-perfect economy. This is a genuine comedy classic from this film.

jokes.text: Ron trying to calm Veronica in the bear pit: 'It's all right. I think it's all right, my sweet chinchilla.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Veronica are surrounded by bears.
jokes.punchline: 'My sweet chinchilla' — Ron's term of endearment in an existentially dangerous moment is a completely wrong animal for the situation (they're in a bear pit) and an absurd non sequitur pet name that reveals Ron's mind is not entirely present.
jokes.explanation: 'My sweet chinchilla' is a great absurdist detail — the specificity of choosing 'chinchilla' (a small, fluffy, entirely bear-unrelated animal) is exactly right. Ron's endearments throughout the film are always off-kilter; this one is particularly well-chosen for maximum absurdity given the context.

jokes.text: In the bear pit, Ron demands to know the truth about the teleprompter: Veronica starts to confess, Ron interrupts: 'Sweet Eli Whitney's nose! It wasn't you, was it?'
jokes.setup: Ron is about to learn the truth about who sabotaged his teleprompter.
jokes.punchline: Ron's expletive of choice — 'Sweet Eli Whitney's nose!' — is a completely novel and baffling historical oath that tells you everything about Ron's brain: he swears by irrelevant 18th century inventors.
jokes.explanation: Ron's idiosyncratic pseudo-profanity ('Great Odin's raven,' 'By the hammer of Thor') is one of the film's signature comedic devices, and 'Sweet Eli Whitney's nose' is among the best of them. The specific choice of Eli Whitney — inventor of the cotton gin — is brilliantly arbitrary. The 'nose' makes it even stranger. High originality; this could only be Ron Burgundy in 1970s America.

jokes.text: Bear roars — Veronica: 'You woke the bears. Why did you do that?'
jokes.setup: Ron/Veronica's argument has apparently woken the bears.
jokes.punchline: Veronica's accusatory 'Why did you do that?' — as if waking sleeping bears in a pit you're trapped in was a deliberate lifestyle choice — is perfectly calm and mildly accusatory.
jokes.explanation: Good economy joke. The 'why did you do that' framing implies Ron had a choice in whether to wake the bears, which is absurd. Slight understatement in the delivery makes it work. Brisk and effective.

jokes.text: Ron, amid bear attack: 'It took my impending death for me to realize how much I need you.'
jokes.setup: Bears are approaching. Ron chooses this moment for a romantic declaration.
jokes.punchline: The rom-com sincerity of 'it took my impending death' is funny because (a) the impending death is not figurative and (b) Ron uses a cliché romantic revelation formula in the most inappropriate possible context, completely sincerely.
jokes.explanation: Decent joke riding the tension between genre conventions (romantic declaration) and literal bear attack. Ron's sincerity makes it land. The 'impending death' acknowledgment is funnier than if he'd used a softer word.

jokes.text: News team member (Champ?) after witnessing bears approaching: 'News team, let's hunt.' Everyone assembles to fight the bears.
jokes.setup: Ron and Veronica are in danger in the bear pit.
jokes.punchline: The news team — anchors, reporters, cameramen — deciding to 'hunt' the bears is entirely absurd. 'Let's hunt' spoken with total authority by a sportscaster treats bear combat as a natural extension of their job description.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the bear fight sequence. 'Let's hunt' has a beautiful macho absurdity — Champ Kind is a sportscaster, so hunting is at least in his conceptual vocabulary, making it funnier than if Brian said it. Effectively kicks off one of the film's most anarchic sequences.

jokes.text: 'Bear fight!'
jokes.setup: The news team arrives to rescue Ron and Veronica from bears
jokes.punchline: Champ's battle cry is simply 'Bear fight!' — delivered with the same enthusiasm as 'Let's get 'em!' for a sporting event
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum economy, perfect Champ Kind energy. His sports announcer frame applied to literal bear combat is both funny and characterful. The simplicity is the strength — it doesn't explain or elaborate, it just commits.

jokes.text: During the bear fight: 'Hit 'em in the uvula!'
jokes.setup: News team is in hand-to-paw combat with bears.
jokes.punchline: The anatomical specificity of 'uvula' — the dangly throat thing — as the targeted weak point for a bear is so particular and medical-sounding that it becomes hilarious. It implies someone has strategized about optimal bear uvula strikes.
jokes.explanation: Four words, completely original. 'Hit 'em in the uvula!' is the perfect absurdist bear-fighting advice — it sounds like it could be real tactical knowledge while being entirely useless and oddly specific. High economy, high originality. Classic McKay improvisation energy.

jokes.text: In the middle of the bear fight, Brick shouts happily: 'Hey, Ron! I'm riding a furry tractor!'
jokes.setup: News team is fighting giant bears — a life-threatening situation.
jokes.punchline: Brick, apparently mounted on a bear, describes his experience as 'riding a furry tractor' — a joyful agricultural metaphor that reveals he has completely misread the situation as fun rather than life-threatening.
jokes.explanation: Among the best lines in the film and in this reel. 'Furry tractor' is a genuinely original comedic construction — it describes a bear perfectly from the perspective of someone who has no context for what a bear is experientially, while also being the exact thing Brick Tamland would say. It's character-specific to a degree almost nothing else in the film matches: only Brick, with his unique cognitive profile, would reach for 'furry tractor.' The joy in the delivery ('Hey, Ron!') adds to the absurdity. This is a 9+ moment.

jokes.text: Brian Fantana, mid-bear-fight, shouts: 'I'm riding a furry tractor!'
jokes.setup: Brian is fighting a bear — apparently mounted on its back
jokes.punchline: 'Furry tractor' as a description of a bear being ridden is both a terrible and perfect simile — it captures the physicality (slow, large, powerful) while being completely wrong as a vehicle metaphor
jokes.explanation: One of the great single-line absurdist jokes of the film. 'Furry tractor' is impossible to predict and impossible to forget — it's wrong in every way (tractors don't have fur; bears are not vehicles) but oddly accurate as a tactile description. The specificity of 'tractor' rather than any other vehicle is what makes it brilliant. This is 8+ material: original, economical, memorable, and could only exist in Anchorman.

jokes.text: Ron narrating his own death during the bear fight: 'The bears have descended on the news team and it's not going well. Clearly, after today, I will no longer—' interrupted by a bear. 'Come on! Oh, God! It's getting to be ri-goddamn-diculous!'
jokes.setup: Ron is in active physical combat with bears.
jokes.punchline: Ron narrates the bear attack in anchor-style, beginning a formal sign-off mid-fight ('Clearly, after today, I will no longer—') before being physically interrupted. His conclusion — 'ri-goddamn-diculous' — is both his folksy idiom and a word that sounds like it was invented by a news anchor.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. Ron cannot stop being an anchor even while being attacked by bears — he auto-narrates his own death in broadcast style. 'Clearly, after today, I will no longer—' is structurally brilliant: it's the beginning of a proper anchor sign-off interrupted by a bear, suggesting Ron was going to formally conclude his career on camera even here. 'Ri-goddamn-diculous' is a perfect Ron Burgundy profanity. This scores 8+ because only Ron Burgundy exists in this register.

jokes.text: Voice in the bear pit: 'Oh, no. We woke up the mama.'
jokes.setup: The bear fight has already been chaos — bears everywhere.
jokes.punchline: The calm, matter-of-fact 'we woke up the mama' is delivered as if the situation just got measurably worse in a way that was preventable — escalating the bear threat to its logical maximum.
jokes.explanation: Classic horror-movie escalation beat used for comedy. 'We woke up the mama' is effectively terrifying and funny in equal measure. The understatement of the delivery ('oh, no') is correct. Not a novel construction but executed crisply.

jokes.text: In the most desperate moment of the bear attack, Baxter the dog appears and communicates with the bears, leading them away.
jokes.setup: Everyone is about to be killed by bears, including mama bear. There is no escape.
jokes.punchline: Baxter — Ron's dog — apparently speaks bear language and negotiates their safe passage. The resolution of a life-threatening bear attack by a dog diplomat is surreal and committed to completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The Baxter bear-language resolution is both structurally satisfying (Baxter has been built up as a remarkable dog throughout) and completely absurdist (dog diplomacy with bears). Its commitment — no winking at the camera, just the bears following Baxter away — elevates it. The long setup for Baxter across the film makes this a well-earned payoff.

jokes.text: Ron reunites with Baxter, alive and well: 'Oh, Baxter! Oh! Oh, Baxter, you're still alive! I'm so happy! I'm so happy! You are alive! I'm so happy! I will lick you! I will lick you in front of everyone to show my joy.'
jokes.setup: Ron believed Baxter was dead. The dog is alive.
jokes.punchline: Ron's escalating declarations of joy become more unhinged with each repetition, culminating in the offer to lick the dog publicly 'in front of everyone' — a vow of affection so animal that it inverts the man/dog relationship.
jokes.explanation: 'I will lick you in front of everyone to show my joy' is a great escalation from normal dog-owner delight to something primal and absurd. The specificity of 'in front of everyone' — as if public licking carries more emotional weight — is an ideal Ron Burgundy detail. His relationship with Baxter is one of the film's funniest ongoing elements.

jokes.text: Wes Mantooth confronts Ron: 'Deep down in my stomach, with every inch of me, I pure, straight hate you! But, God damn it, do I respect you!'
jokes.setup: Wes Mantooth has been Ron's professional nemesis throughout the film. He approaches after the bear pit crisis.
jokes.punchline: The misdirection: 'I pure, straight hate you!' promises a climactic villain confrontation, then immediately pivots to 'do I respect you!' The hatred and respect are delivered with equal passion, making the respect as devastating an admission as the hate.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. 'I pure, straight hate you' is itself a funny formulation ('pure, straight' as intensifiers), but the pivot to 'God damn it, do I respect you!' is the real craft. The phrasing 'God damn it, do I' implies the respect is unwanted, admitted against his will — and the equal passion makes both emotions more absurd. Very quotable, well-structured misdirection.

jokes.text: Ron responds to Mantooth's hate-respect declaration: 'Thank you, brother.' Then a long, earnest handshake/embrace while the crowd chants 'Burgundy!'
jokes.setup: Wes has just admitted to hating Ron.
jokes.punchline: Ron receives the hate-respect declaration with 'Thank you, brother' — the warm sincerity of accepting a compliment you don't quite deserve. The subsequent crowd chanting escalates the absurdity of a rivalry ending with a brotherly embrace.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the Mantooth rivalry. 'Thank you, brother' as a response to being told you're hated is exactly Ron's register — he processes the compliment and ignores the insult, because that's what Ron does. Crowd chanting adds to the mock-epic quality of the ending.

jokes.text: After the reconciliation, Mantooth calls Ron 'brother' and they embrace
jokes.setup: Mantooth has just confessed he hates but respects Ron
jokes.punchline: The instantaneous leap from 'I hate you' to 'brother' and a full embrace is played as emotional whiplash — the audience registers that Mantooth has completely capitulated in about fifteen seconds
jokes.explanation: Functional coda to the previous joke. The 'brother' beats on the speed of the emotional flip rather than any new comedic content. Works as punctuation but isn't a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Ed Harken announcing Ron's return: 'Today we spell redemption R-O-N.'
jokes.setup: Ron is being welcomed back as a hero.
jokes.punchline: Harken — who has spent the film visibly resenting Ron — delivers an over-the-top PR proclamation of Ron's redemption with what sounds like sincere enthusiasm, suggesting that in news management, all is forgiven if the ratings are good.
jokes.explanation: Pleasant but fairly conventional 'big speech' joke. The spelling-out-redemption move is a little obvious. Works as crowd moment but isn't particularly crafted comedy.

jokes.text: Ron begins his triumphant broadcast: '...ever to happen to San Diago or even the world.'
jokes.setup: Ron is delivering what should be his finest, most professional broadcast
jokes.punchline: He mispronounces/misspells 'San Diego' as 'San Diago' — in his greatest moment, his fundamental incompetence reasserts itself
jokes.explanation: A quiet but well-placed character joke — Ron getting the name of his own city wrong in his moment of greatest triumph. It's a small callback to Ron's fundamental unreliability that doesn't undercut the emotional beat but adds an ironic layer.

jokes.text: During the live broadcast, Brick wanders in front of the camera: 'High-pressure system—' Ron: 'No, no, no, no, Brick. High-pressure system— Go stand over there.'
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to do a professional live report with Veronica.
jokes.punchline: Brick — apparently having prepared weather content — begins delivering an unrelated forecast on the live feed. Ron has to physically redirect him mid-broadcast.
jokes.explanation: Good Brick comedy — he's prepared a weather report for a panda birth story and sees no issue with this. 'Go stand over there' is Ron's patient-but-exasperated management of Brick throughout the film. Character specific and consistent.

jokes.text: Veronica's declaration of love to Ron on live TV: 'Ron, there are literally thousands of men that I should be with instead, but I am 72% sure that I love you.'
jokes.setup: Ron has invited Veronica to co-anchor with him on live television — a romantic gesture in his universe.
jokes.punchline: 'I am 72% sure that I love you' — the journalistic precision applied to romantic declaration. Veronica has been trained to caveat everything with accuracy; she gives love a confidence interval.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel and possibly the film. 'I am 72% sure that I love you' is a genuinely original construction: it takes the journalistic precision that defines Veronica's character and applies it to the most unquantifiable human emotion. The specificity of '72%' (not 'pretty sure,' not 'fairly certain,' but 72%) gives it the authority of a poll result. It's also genuinely romantic in a broken, accurate way — she IS telling him she loves him, just within appropriate confidence intervals. The setup ('literally thousands of men I should be with instead') makes the punchline land harder by raising the stakes. This scores 8.75 because it's exceptional character-specific comedy with high originality and near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Narrator's epilogue: 'Champ Kind went on to become a commentator for the NFL, but was later fired after being accused of sexual harassment by Terry Bradshaw.'
jokes.setup: The narrator begins wrapping up what happened to each news team member after the events of the film.
jokes.punchline: Champ's outcome — sexual harassment accusation by Terry Bradshaw specifically — is both completely in character (Champ's aggressive masculinity throughout the film) and funny because Terry Bradshaw is a named real person, adding specificity.
jokes.explanation: Good epilogue joke. Using Terry Bradshaw — an NFL legend — as the harassment victim subverts the expected power dynamic (usually a powerful man harassing someone less powerful). Champ being fired from football commentary for harassing Terry Bradshaw is a great dark punchline. Well-integrated into Champ's established character.

jokes.text: During Champ's epilogue, he approaches the narrator or another character and says: 'Excuse me. Is that Sex Panther you're wearing?'
jokes.setup: The film is in its epilogue narration.
jokes.punchline: Champ is literally doing the thing he was just accused of — inappropriate workplace behavior using Sex Panther cologne as a pretext — to someone off-screen, in the middle of his own narrated downfall.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: the narrator has just said Champ was fired for harassment, and Champ immediately demonstrates why. The Sex Panther callback rewards attentive viewers. The simultaneity of narration and action is a smart meta-structural joke — his behavior IS the evidence for the narrator's claim. High character integration: Champ would absolutely do this. This is the best of the epilogue jokes.

jokes.text: Brian Fantana epilogue: 'went on to have great success as the host of the hit reality TV show "Intercourse Island" on the Fox Network.'
jokes.setup: The narrator wraps up Brian's fate.
jokes.punchline: 'Intercourse Island' on Fox — a parody of reality TV excess that speaks directly to Brian's established character as a womanizer who has 'the most powerful cologne in the world.' Of course Brian ended up on a Fox sex-reality show. The specificity of naming Fox is the right level of satirical edge.
jokes.explanation: 'Intercourse Island' is a great fake show name — specific, slightly disgusting, and perfect for Fox. Brian hosting a sex reality show is exactly his logical endpoint. Character-specific and well-constructed.

jokes.text: Narrator announces: 'Brick Tamland is married with 11 children and is one of the top political advisors to the Bush White House.' While Brick is shown tickling someone and shouting 'I'm gonna get you! I'm gonna get you!'
jokes.setup: The narrator wraps up Brick's post-film fate.
jokes.punchline: The gap between 'top political advisor to the Bush White House' and the visual of Brick gleefully playing chase is enormous and pointed. The joke implies the Bush White House's decision-making quality, while also being perfectly consistent with Brick's established intelligence level.
jokes.explanation: Excellent satirical joke. The contrast between narrator's authoritative claim and what we're watching Brick do is a perfect visual/verbal split joke. The Bush White House reference is specific enough to be biting political satire without being preachy. 11 children is an absurd number that tells you more about Brick's lack of planning skills. Strong character integration — Brick as political advisor is funny precisely because we've spent 90 minutes learning exactly how limited his cognition is.

jokes.text: Ron and Veronica's final broadcast sign-off: Ron: 'You stay classy, planet Earth.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Veronica have become the first mixed-gender network news team and are signing off their broadcast.
jokes.punchline: 'Stay classy, planet Earth' — escalating from 'Stay classy, San Diego' (his sign-off throughout the film) to 'planet Earth' as Ron's ego expands to match his new network status.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character arc joke. 'Stay classy, San Diego' has been Ron's signature throughout the film; upgrading it to 'planet Earth' is exactly the right escalation that tells Ron's entire story in three words. He's gone from local to global and his ego has updated accordingly. Highly quotable, strong callback payoff, great economy. This is what a good final joke looks like — it completes a running gag while also being funny on its own.

jokes.text: During the credits outtake sequence, characters hit/experience something and shout: 'Great Odin's raven!' / 'By the hammer of Thor!' / 'Saint Damien's beard!' / 'Sweet grandmother's spatula!' / 'Hot pot of coffee!' / 'Uncle Jonathan's corncob pipe!'
jokes.setup: Outtake/gag reel sequence during credits showing characters reacting to painful moments.
jokes.punchline: Ron's pseudo-profanity continues to escalate through increasingly absurd historical/domestic objects: 'grandmother's spatula,' 'corncob pipe,' each one more mundane and inexplicable than the last.
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Ron's profanity reaching maximum absurdity in the outtakes is the ideal capper for this character device. 'Sweet grandmother's spatula' and 'Uncle Jonathan's corncob pipe' are especially good — the domestic specificity ('Uncle Jonathan' — not just any corncob pipe) makes these feel like actual memories Ron has that he's weaponized as oaths. This is a running gag that earns its escalation.

jokes.text: Outtake: someone threatens 'I'm gonna shoot you with a BB gun when you're not looking. In the back of the head. I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Outtake/improvised threat sequence.
jokes.punchline: The threat escalates to 'in the back of the head' — a genuinely menacing image — immediately undercut by 'I'm sorry,' suggesting the person is both threatening violence and apologetic about it simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Good dark-absurdist construction: 'in the back of the head' adds specificity that makes it more threatening, then 'I'm sorry' deflates it immediately. The apology implies pre-emptive guilt for a planned sniper attack. Solid outtake humor.

jokes.text: Outtake: 'You're not very bright. You know that, right? You're actually quite a dullard. Everyone here knows it.' Response: 'If I'm a dullard, you're the, uh, the dull—' 'Oh! Can't think of anything to say, can you?' 'Yes, I can. I can think of a lot of things to say. Like, you're a dirty bitch.'
jokes.setup: Outtake sequence, apparently Ron being called slow-witted.
jokes.punchline: Ron's attempt to form a comeback ('you're the, uh, the dull—') fails in real time, then he defensively claims he CAN think of things, then produces 'you're a dirty bitch' — which is the best he has after a full pause. The failure of wit followed by insistence he has wit, confirmed by an extremely basic insult.
jokes.explanation: Very good character comedy outtake. Ron demonstrating his own limited wit while claiming to have wit is classic comic irony. The extended pause before 'you're a dirty bitch' — which he delivers with apparent pride — is structurally excellent. The heckler's 'Oh! Can't think of anything to say, can you?' just before Ron produces his comeback makes the comeback funnier. High character integration: this is exactly how Ron's mind works.

jokes.text: Outtake: 'Well, Ron, I'm gonna put poison—' Ron: 'Oh, my God!'
jokes.setup: Someone begins a threat: 'I'm gonna put poison—'
jokes.punchline: Ron's reaction ('Oh, my God!') comes before the sentence is finished — he reacts to 'poison' alone before learning where the poison is going, suggesting this is a threat familiar enough in Ron's world that the word alone triggers alarm.
jokes.explanation: Quick outtake beat. The interrupted threat with the premature reaction is funny but brief. The joke is in Ron's pre-emptive horror at the word 'poison' alone. Light but functional.

jokes.text: Outtake: 'I drank a lava lamp. It wasn't lava.' / 'I ate a whole bunch of fiberglass insulation. It wasn't cotton candy like that guy said. My stomach's itchy.'
jokes.setup: Brick is in the outtake sequence, apparently confessing to recent dietary choices.
jokes.punchline: Brick has consumed both a lava lamp's contents AND fiberglass insulation, in both cases misled by others. 'It wasn't cotton candy like that guy said' implies someone tricked Brick into eating insulation. 'My stomach's itchy' is a perfect understatement of the medical consequences.
jokes.explanation: Among the best Brick moments in the film. 'It wasn't cotton candy like that guy said' implies a whole world of Brick being deceived into eating hazardous materials by unnamed individuals who apparently make a habit of this. 'My stomach's itchy' is the perfect medical understatement for fiberglass ingestion. The lava lamp/fiberglass double-entry is an escalation that follows the logic of Brick's mind: he tried a lava lamp, didn't learn his lesson, tried insulation. Character integration is essentially perfect — only Brick could have experienced these things with this narrative tone.

jokes.text: Brick continues: 'I pooped a hammer. I pooped a tape recorder. I pooped a Cornish game hen.'
jokes.setup: Brick has just confessed to eating lava lamp fluid and fiberglass insulation.
jokes.punchline: The list of items Brick has apparently defecated is a perfect escalation: hammer (hard, painful-sounding), tape recorder (inexplicable object to have ingested), Cornish game hen (food item that traveled through intact). The specificity of 'Cornish game hen' is the comedic peak.
jokes.explanation: One of the funniest moments in the entire film and the comedic peak of this reel. The triple escalation of impossible objects Brick has excreted is structurally perfect: hammer is shocking, tape recorder is surreal, 'Cornish game hen' is the perfect absurdist specific — not 'chicken,' but a Cornish GAME HEN, implying a certain level of culinary specificity in Brick's consumption. The calm, matter-of-fact delivery of three items as though they were items on a grocery list is exactly right. This is calibrated against the 'furry tractor' and 'milk was a bad choice' lines and matches or exceeds them.

jokes.text: Outtake: 'You do not take a tone with me, 'cause I will give you a rap right on the Jack Johnson!' — then immediately: 'Now this is happenin'. What are you doing? Hah! What are you doing? What are you—'
jokes.setup: Ron is threatening someone in the outtake sequence.
jokes.punchline: 'I will give you a rap right on the Jack Johnson' — a euphemism for a groin strike, using a historical boxing champion's name as the anatomical placeholder — is both archaic and specific. 'Now this is happenin'' as a sudden announcement of his own dance/fight move is a perfect non sequitur.
jokes.explanation: 'Jack Johnson' as a groin euphemism is clever and period-appropriate for Ron's 1970s register. 'Now this is happenin'' as a self-announcement of physical action is a great absurdist detail. Good character integration — Ron threatening people in an unnecessarily formal/archaic register is consistent.

jokes.text: Outtake: actors flubbing lines and bickering over who says what. Ron/Will Ferrell: 'I guess we'll go back to doing what I do best, show off. When do we get started?' Other actor: 'That's my line.' Ron: 'When do we get started?' Other: 'You say, Whenever you like.' Ron: 'Whenever you like.' Director: 'Keep it rollin'. This is good stuff.'
jokes.setup: The outtake reel shows actors mid-scene losing track of their lines.
jokes.punchline: The director's 'Keep it rollin'. This is good stuff' — keeping the camera rolling on what is clearly not good stuff — is the meta joke. The confusion is played as a real outtake while the director's enthusiasm for it is ironic.
jokes.explanation: Meta outtake humor. This is a relatively weak moment compared to the Brick jokes surrounding it — it's the standard 'actors flubbing lines' gag. The director's 'this is good stuff' is the best element. Functions as palate cleanser between stronger bits.

jokes.text: Outtake: 'Brick, before I let you go, are you still having your celebrity golf tournament this summer?' Brick: 'No, too many people died last year. So we're not gonna do—' then breaks: 'Sorry. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: Ron asks Brick about a golf tournament in a conversational outtake exchange.
jokes.punchline: 'Too many people died last year' — apparently Brick's charity golf tournament has a mortality problem serious enough to cancel it. This is delivered completely straight before Brick breaks character.
jokes.explanation: Very funny dark improvisation. 'Too many people died last year' is exactly the kind of Brick improvisation that makes the film great — it implies a golf tournament that is somehow lethal enough that cancellation was the right call. The 'So we're not gonna do—' trailing off before the break adds to the charm. High quotability as a standalone line.

jokes.text: Outtake: 'They named it San Diego. Which in German means, "a whale's vagina."'
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining the etymology of 'San Diego' in an outtake (and earlier said 'San Diago' in his broadcast, joke #49).
jokes.punchline: San Diego does not mean 'whale's vagina' in German or in any language. Ron's confident false etymology — delivered as authoritative fact — is the joke. The specificity of 'whale's vagina' as the false meaning is maximally absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and a certified Anchorman classic. 'A whale's vagina' is the ideal absurdist false etymology — it's specific, anatomically precise, biologically real (whales do have them), and completely unexpected as a city name meaning. Ron's authoritative delivery of completely wrong information is his core character comedy, and this is its purest expression. The word choice 'vagina' rather than a euphemism is exactly right — Ron's pseudo-academic register demands clinical terminology. This is a 9+ moment on quotability and very close to it on craft.

jokes.text: Post-credits: 'We are laughing! And we are very good friends. Good buddies sharing a special moment. Don't say anything, Ron. Just let it happen. We're laughing, enjoying our friendship. And someday we'll look back on this with much fondness.'
jokes.setup: Post-credits outtake: two characters are ostensibly sharing a friendly laugh.
jokes.punchline: Narrating the laughter while laughing — 'We are laughing!' — treats the spontaneous moment as something that needs to be formally documented and preserved even as it happens. The instructions ('Don't say anything, Ron. Just let it happen.') imply the moment is fragile and might escape if not carefully managed.
jokes.explanation: 'We are laughing!' as a meta-announcement of laughter — narrating the moment to preserve it — is a smart final joke. The gentle comedy of treating a spontaneous friendship moment as a formal occasion ('Don't say anything, Ron. Just let it happen') is warmly absurd. 'Someday we'll look back on this with much fondness' as an immediate future-tense nostalgia framing is a nice touch. Good closing beat.
